\chapter{Tener in the Plural, and the Stem-Change Rule}
\label{ch:spanish-tener-plural}
\hlchaptermodality{56}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use tener in every person, and state when a stem changes and when it does not.}

The stem breaks exactly where it is stressed - so nosotros and vosotros never break, in any verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tenemos · tenéis]{tenemos — and the stem change disappears}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-tenemos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}you have.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Tengo, tienes}.) And \textquotedblleft{}we eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Comemos}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the break is gone}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{tenemos} — \emph{we have.}  ·  \textbf{tenéis} — \emph{you all have.}
\end{quote}

Not \emph{tienemos}. Look at what happened: \emph{tienes} had the broken stem \textbf{ie}, and here it is plain \textbf{e} again — the ordinary \emph{-er} endings, on the ordinary stem.

\textbf{You already know why.} It is the same reason \texttt{-er} and \texttt{-ir} looked identical in the singular and parted in the plural: \textbf{stress}.

\emph{Tienes} stresses the stem, and a stressed \textbf{e} in that position breaks into \textbf{ie}. \emph{Tenemos} stresses the \emph{ending}, so the stem is unstressed and its vowel stays whole.

The stem change was never a property of the verb. It is a property of \textbf{where the stress lands}, and these two forms are where the stress lands elsewhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tienes\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}tenemos\textquotedblright{} — and hear the stress move off the stem
  \item \textquotedblleft{}comemos, tenemos\textquotedblright{} — the same endings
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}we have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Tenemos}.) Where did the \textbf{ie} go? (Nowhere — it only ever appears when the \textbf{stem} is stressed.) Next: the form where the stress comes back.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tienen]{tienen — the break comes back}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-tienen}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we have\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}you have\textquotedblright{} to a friend. (\emph{Tenemos, tienes}.) Which one has the broken stem?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the rule, stated once and for all}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{tienen} — \emph{they have}, and \textbf{ustedes tienen}, \emph{you all have}.
\end{quote}

The \textbf{ie} is back. And now you have seen it appear, vanish and return, which is enough to state the rule outright:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A stem change happens exactly where the stem is stressed, and nowhere else.}
\end{quote}

That is four forms with the break — setting aside the \emph{yo} form, which has an oddity of its own — and two without: \emph{nosotros} and \emph{vosotros}. Always those two. In every stem-changing verb in the language.

Learners are usually told to memorise a shape called \textquotedblleft{}the boot\textquotedblright{} — the four stressed forms drawn as an outline around a table. \textbf{You do not need the boot.} You need to know where Spanish puts its stress, which you already do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tienes, tenemos, tienen\textquotedblright{} — break, no break, break
  \item the two forms that never break, for any verb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}they have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Tienen}.) State the stem-change rule. (\textbf{The stem breaks exactly where it is stressed.}) Which two forms never break? (\emph{Nosotros} and \emph{vosotros}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
